newsitem.title: INDIA: Hostages' families to go to Kashmir amid pessimism.
newsitem.headline: Hostages' families to go to Kashmir amid pessimism.

text.p: Relatives of three Westerners held hostage in Kashmir for more than a year plan to travel to the Himalayan region amid what Britain's ambassador called increasing pessimism over the captive tourists' fate.
Diplomats said the father and girlfriend of British hostage Paul Wells, as well as the wife of his compatriot Keith Mangan, were set to arrive in India on Sunday.
Jane Schelly, wife of U.S. hostage Donald Hutchings, was expected to arrive in the next day or two, they said.
All of the relatives planned to visit Kashmir, where the four hostages were kidnapped by Al-Faran guerrillas in July 1995, the diplomats said.
Hutchings, Mangan and Wells were captured with American John Childs on July 4, 1995 while trekking in the Himalayan mountains.
Childs escaped four days later, and Al-Faran militants kidnapped German Dirk Hasert and Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe on the same day. Ostroe was found beheaded in a Kashmiri forest in August 1995.
Indian authorities have not had contact with Al-Faran since last November, and diplomats said they had no firm information to indicate whether the hostages are dead or alive.
Authorities using sniffer dogs recently scoured a forest where a captured militant said he believed the hostages had been buried after being killed last year. But the search turned up no clues.
The United States is considering offering a financial reward for information about the whereabouts of the hostages, diplomats said last week.
But Washington wanted first to clear the offer with Indian authorities and the other countries whose nationals are held.
British High Commissioner (ambassador) David Gore-Booth told reporters on Thursday that there were reports that the hostages had recently been sighted.
But he said there was no firm information as to their whereabouts. "We have no proof of life or proof of death," he said.
Asked if diplomats were extremely gloomy, Gore-Booth said: "Yes."
The British envoy said the hostages' relatives were coming to assess the situation themselves. "We have let it be known to them that we are increasingly pessimistic," he said.
Gore-Booth said the hostages' families had not been told to assume their relatives had been killed, nor were diplomats raising false hopes.
The British hostages' relatives planned to cooperate in the production of a documentary for television which a diplomat said aimed at "securing publicity for their loved ones' plight".
"An opportunity is being seized," the diplomat said.
